title: Analyst briefing dry run - Production economics benchmark (latency/$)
summary: Internal dry run for the upcoming analyst briefing on Redwood’s public-facing “production economics” benchmark report. Team rehearsed the opening narrative, walked through methodology guardrails (variance, caching/batching policy, region comparability), and practiced responses to anticipated analyst pushback (cherry-picking, vendor bias, hardware variability, real-world workload mismatch). Action items focus on tightening disclaimers, aligning on what claims are allowed, and preparing a short “repro steps” appendix and Q&A one-pagers for Sales/SE follow-up.
topics: Briefing structure and roles (who covers market framing vs methodology vs GTM)
Definitions: latency/$, throughput/cost, p50 vs p95, confidence language
Methodology constraints: warmup, caching policy, concurrency distributions, time windows
Region comparability and data residency questions
Competitive framing and “so what” for buyers
Reproducibility and what will/won’t be published publicly
Objection handling: cherry-picking, benchmark vs real workload, pricing assumptions
Launch motions: landing page, CTAs, follow-up for Dedicated/Private evaluations
questions: What exactly are we claiming as “better”: latency/$, absolute latency, or reliability under load?
How do we explain that results may differ for different prompt mixes and context lengths without undermining the report?
If an analyst asks for raw logs or per-request traces, what’s the approved answer?
How do we respond if a competitor publishes a conflicting benchmark the same week?
action_items: Soojin Lee - Tighten “do/don’t” language for comparative claims; add two approved comparison sentences and two non-approved examples - due 2025-02-21
Claire Dubois - Provide a 3-bullet explanation of caching/batching policy and why it’s realistic (and what it’s not) - due 2025-02-21
Sana Farid - Add one slide note with variance ranges + rerun triggers wording (no hard numbers if not approved) - due 2025-02-21
Ethan Wallace - Insert a 30-second “how to read the charts” script for p50 vs p95 and latency/$ - due 2025-02-21
Markus Klein - Draft a one-page Q&A for SEs: reproducing the benchmark (region header, config flags, expected deltas) - due 2025-02-24
Ben Carter - Confirm which CTAs are on the analyst landing page vs report PDF; align UTM naming for analyst follow-ups - due 2025-02-24
Talia Benson - Send updated run-of-show with timeboxes and speaker handoffs; schedule 15-min final run on Monday - due 2025-02-21
next_steps: Update analyst deck speaker notes to reflect approved claims/disclaimers
Finalize the Q&A cheat sheet for anticipated hard questions (raw data, pricing assumptions, hardware, region deltas)
One more timed rehearsal focused on fast, consistent answers (no over-claiming)
Confirm who answers “security/data handling” questions in the live briefing (Camila vs Jonas vs Jordan)
transcript:
Redwood Inference - Fireflies Transcript

Title: Analyst briefing dry run - Production economics benchmark (latency/$)
Date: 2025-02-20 5:00 PM PT
Duration: 47 min
Attendees: Jordan Blake, Camila Reyes, Ben Carter, Soojin Lee, Ethan Wallace, Jonas Weber, Claire Dubois, Sana Farid, Markus Klein, Talia Benson

AUTO SUMMARY (generated)
- Purpose: practice analyst briefing narrative + handle pushback questions
- Focus areas: methodology credibility, variance language, what we will publish, competitive framing, and next-step motions


[00:00] Talia Benson: Cool, we’re at the top. This is the dry run for the analyst briefing. Goal is, uh, keep it tight to 25 minutes of content, 20 minutes Q&A. We’re recording so we can pull exact phrasing.

[00:14] Jordan Blake: Awesome. I’ll run point as if the analyst is on. Camila, you kick with the market framing. Jonas you take methodology. Ben and Ethan you can jump for the “so what” and the report assets. Markus, you’re our “hard question” person.

[00:31] Camila Reyes: Yep. Okay.

[00:33] Jordan Blake: One reminder—no numbers we haven’t approved in the deck. If someone asks, we say, “we can follow up” versus improvising.

[00:41] Soojin Lee: And no “we’re the best” language. We can say “we aim to be the reference” and “here’s how we controlled for X.”

[00:48] Jordan Blake: Great. Camila, go.

[00:52] Camila Reyes: Thanks everyone for joining. The headline is: as open models proliferate, performance differences are increasingly about serving—latency, reliability, and cost. What we’re publishing is a benchmark report focused on production economics, specifically latency per dollar, broken down by model family and region.

[01:12] Camila Reyes: The reason analysts and buyers care is procurement is asking, “what’s my cost per output token at my SLO?” Engineering is asking, “can I hit p95 under load?” And platform teams are asking for repeatability across regions and deployment modes.

[01:30] Ben Carter: (quiet) Can you add the line about “not just cost-only” here?

[01:33] Camila Reyes: Yeah—this is not a cheapest-token contest. We’re pairing latency and cost so people can understand tradeoffs.

[01:43] Jordan Blake: Okay, pause. That opening is good. Minor tweak: call out “throughput per dollar” as a supporting metric, but keep the hero metric as latency/$.

[01:52] Camila Reyes: Got it.

[01:55] Jordan Blake: Jonas, you’re up: methodology overview in like, four minutes.

[02:00] Jonas Weber: Sure. So, methodology: we define two baseline workloads—chat completions and embeddings. For each, we run a fixed distribution of input lengths and output lengths that match common production shapes, and we run at set concurrency levels.

[02:18] Jonas Weber: We collect p50 and p95 latency, throughput, and metered cost for the run window. Then we compute latency/$ in a consistent way per model and per region.

[02:30] Claire Dubois: Jonas, just say “same harness across regions” explicitly.

[02:33] Jonas Weber: Yes—same harness, same configuration, same run windows across regions, to the extent cloud capacity allows.

[02:41] Sana Farid: And say “repeat runs.” That’s where we get variance.

[02:44] Jonas Weber: Right. We do repeated runs and apply rerun triggers if variance or noise exceeds thresholds. We don’t publish single-shot results.

[02:55] Jordan Blake: Good. Now do the part everyone asks: caching and batching. Keep it honest.

[03:01] Jonas Weber: Sure. We apply a warm-up period to avoid cold-start artifacts. For caching: we do not do special prompt-prefix caching that would advantage a specific prompt set. For batching: we use the platform’s normal continuous batching behavior—representative of how customers run for cost efficiency—while ensuring we don’t violate the latency targets.

[03:23] Markus Klein: I’d tighten that: analysts will hear “we tuned it to look good.” Say “the runtime defaults used in production,” not “normal-ish.”

[03:30] Jonas Weber: Good point. The wording should be: “We use production runtime defaults and document any deviations.”

[03:38] Soojin Lee: And if there are deviations, we state them as “for measurement consistency,” not “optimization.”

[03:44] Ethan Wallace: Also we should have the line that these are not synthetic microbenchmarks; it’s end-to-end API latency including queueing under load, right?

[03:52] Claire Dubois: Yes. End-to-end as seen by a client. But no internet path variance—we run clients in-region.

[04:00] Jordan Blake: Great. Okay, let’s run a pretend Q&A. Markus, be the analyst.

[04:06] Markus Klein: Alright. (analyst voice) “So latency per dollar sounds like a made-up metric. Why should I care? Isn’t cost per million tokens enough?”

[04:15] Camila Reyes: I’ll take that. Cost per token alone misses SLOs. Teams don’t buy tokens, they buy user experience at a latency target. Latency/$ captures the combined effect of serving efficiency and the actual response time. If two providers have similar token price but one has better p95 under concurrency, the app is materially different.

[04:38] Markus Klein: (analyst) “But then isn’t it just a ratio you can game by, like, increasing latency to reduce cost?”

[04:45] Jonas Weber: That’s why we report latency and cost separately and include p50 and p95. If someone ‘cheats’ by slowing down, it will show in the latency distribution. The ratio is a summary, not the only data point.

[05:01] Sana Farid: And we should say we keep the workload fixed across runs. So the only degrees of freedom are runtime and infra.

[05:07] Jordan Blake: Good. Next hard one.

[05:10] Markus Klein: (analyst) “Okay. How do I know you didn’t cherry-pick prompts that make you look good?”

[05:17] Claire Dubois: We use prompt distributions designed to represent common production usage—mix of short and long contexts. We’re explicit in the methodology appendix about the distributions and we keep them consistent across models and regions.

[05:33] Markus Klein: (analyst) “Will you publish the full prompt set?”

[05:36] Claire Dubois: We will publish a reproduction guide and a small-scale example harness so teams can run comparable tests. We won’t publish per-request logs or anything that could expose sensitive telemetry. For the prompt set, we can publish representative examples and distributions without dumping the entire internal suite.

[05:55] Soojin Lee: Careful—don’t say “internal suite.” Say “our benchmark suite.”

[05:59] Claire Dubois: Right, sorry.

[06:02] Jordan Blake: And if they push for full prompts, the answer is: “we provide enough to reproduce within reasonable bounds; we balance transparency with operational security.”

[06:12] Markus Klein: (analyst) “You said regions. How do you ensure region-to-region comparability when GPU availability differs?”

[06:20] Sana Farid: We run within defined capacity windows per region and repeat runs. If a region shows instability—like higher variance due to noisy neighbors or capacity contention—we rerun or flag the result. We also include notes where region constraints may affect interpretation.

[06:40] Jonas Weber: And importantly, we don’t compare a best-case region for Redwood to a worst-case region for someone else; the unit of reporting is “model + region” with the same measurement approach.

[06:51] Ben Carter: And we’re explicit that results are “in those regions, at that time.” It’s not a forever guarantee.

[06:58] Markus Klein: (analyst) “So you’re admitting it might change week to week?”

[07:02] Camila Reyes: Performance can vary, yes. That’s why we’re putting emphasis on reproducibility and refresh cadence. The point is to provide a credible reference and a method, not a one-time marketing claim.

[07:19] Jordan Blake: Good. Next question: pricing assumptions. Analysts love this.

[07:24] Markus Klein: (analyst) “Latency per dollar depends on your pricing. Are you using list price? Discounted enterprise contracts? Spot instances? What about committed use?”

[07:33] Ben Carter: We use published pricing for the hosted API where applicable, and for Dedicated/Private we don’t turn it into a spreadsheet war because contracts vary. The benchmark is primarily for hosted, and we frame dedicated as “predictable capacity” rather than a direct price comparison.

[07:53] Jordan Blake: Add: “We can provide a TCO model under NDA for large commitments.” That’s a good follow-up.

[07:59] Soojin Lee: But don’t volunteer it unless asked, because it sounds like we’re hiding something.

[08:03] Jordan Blake: True. Phrase it like: “For enterprise agreements, economics depend on utilization; we can walk through it.”

[08:10] Markus Klein: (analyst) “Okay. And does your cost include networking, storage, control plane fees, engineering time?”

[08:18] Jonas Weber: The cost reported is metered inference cost as billed by Redwood for the endpoint, which reflects compute and the serving stack. It doesn’t include a customer’s own app costs, and we state that clearly.

[08:32] Ethan Wallace: Should we say “it’s the cost you’d see on the invoice,” basically.

[08:35] Jonas Weber: Yes. “Invoice-aligned.”

[08:38] Jordan Blake: Nice phrase: invoice-aligned.

[08:42] Markus Klein: (analyst) “How do you compare to hyperscalers like AWS Bedrock or Vertex?”

[08:48] Camila Reyes: We focus on open model serving economics and the developer experience for running them in production. Hyperscalers provide broad services; our differentiation is a unified inference platform optimized for performance and operational tooling. Where we do comparisons, we stick to apples-to-apples and disclose constraints.

[09:08] Soojin Lee: Add “we don’t speculate on their internals.”

[09:10] Camila Reyes: Right—we only report what we measured, using the described method.

[09:15] Markus Klein: (analyst) “But isn’t this just marketing for your hosted API?”

[09:19] Jordan Blake: It’s a report, yes, but it’s also a stance: the industry needs repeatable production benchmarks. Customers ask us for this data in evaluations, and we’re making it public with disclaimers so teams can make informed decisions.

[09:36] Ethan Wallace: And we’re putting the methodology front-and-center. That’s the credibility piece.

[09:41] Markus Klein: (analyst) “Let’s talk reliability. Your metric ignores downtime and tail spikes.”

[09:47] Jonas Weber: We include p95 latency under load and we run during controlled windows to avoid impacting production. The report is not an SLA document, but we can contextualize results with platform reliability practices—fallbacks, routing, and guardrails.

[10:05] Markus Klein: (analyst) “Do you have error rates?”

[10:08] Claire Dubois: We track them internally and use them as sanity checks. Publicly, we’ll mention that runs with elevated error rates are invalidated and rerun. We’re not publishing error logs.

[10:22] Jordan Blake: Great. Now the spicy one: “are you optimizing for the benchmark.” Markus, ask it.

[10:28] Markus Klein: (analyst) “How do I know Redwood didn’t tweak the runtime just to win this benchmark?”

[10:33] Jonas Weber: Two answers. One: we use production defaults and document configuration used. Two: we have internal guardrails—changes are reviewed and benchmark runs are repeatable. Also, if a runtime improvement helps the benchmark, it helps customers, because the benchmark is end-to-end serving under realistic load.

[10:56] Sana Farid: Add: “We rerun across models and regions; a tweak that only helps one case would show inconsistent effects.”

[11:03] Jonas Weber: Yes, good.

[11:06] Soojin Lee: But do not imply “we never tune.” We do tune—just not for a single competitor. Keep it as “we optimize for production, not for one synthetic test.”

[11:16] Jordan Blake: Right. Wording is everything.

[11:19] Ben Carter: Another tough one is, “Why should I trust your measurement harness?”

[11:24] Claire Dubois: We should say it’s deterministic and versioned. We can provide the harness used for the public run, and we have a sanitized public table generator. (Sorry, too internal.)

[11:36] Ethan Wallace: Just say: “the harness is versioned, run configs are pinned, and results are generated deterministically from run artifacts.”

[11:46] Jordan Blake: Perfect.

[11:48] Talia Benson: Can we do a quick roleplay of the flow? Like, Camila opening, Jonas methods, Ethan findings, then Jordan close.

[11:55] Jordan Blake: Yeah, let’s do a 10-minute run-through without interruptions, then we’ll critique.

[12:02] Camila Reyes: Okay starting. Thanks for joining—today we’re sharing our upcoming benchmark report on production economics: latency per dollar for popular open models across multiple cloud regions. The motivation is simple: as model quality converges, teams win on serving—cost, latency, and reliability—especially at p95 under concurrency.

[12:29] Camila Reyes: We’ve built Redwood as a developer-first inference platform across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. This report is meant to be a credible reference for engineering and procurement teams evaluating open-model inference.

[12:46] Jonas Weber: Methodology: we define workloads for chat and embeddings, with explicit input/output length distributions and concurrency profiles. We run the same harness across regions, with production runtime defaults, warm-up periods, and repeated runs to quantify variance. We report latency (p50, p95), throughput, and invoice-aligned cost, and compute latency/$ as a summary metric.

[13:16] Jonas Weber: Transparency: we publish the method, constraints, and how-to-reproduce guidance, while not disclosing per-request traces or anything sensitive.

[13:28] Ethan Wallace: Findings section: the report breaks down results by model family and region. The key takeaway is not a single winner; it’s that the economics vary materially by region and workload shape, and teams should measure with their own distributions. We provide charts and a table that helps teams shortlist models and regions quickly.

[13:52] Ethan Wallace: We also include guidance on how to interpret p95 vs p50 and why tail latency matters for user-facing apps.

[14:02] Jordan Blake: Close: For teams building production LLM features, we’re making this report available with a landing page and a downloadable PDF. If you want to validate against your workload, we can provide a reproduction template and talk through Dedicated and Private options where capacity and data controls matter.

[14:22] Jordan Blake: End.

[14:25] Talia Benson: Nice. That was 2 minutes in this condensed format; in the real deck it’ll be longer, but the handoffs sounded smooth.

[14:32] Soojin Lee: Camila’s line “as model quality converges” can get challenged. Analysts will say it doesn’t converge for hard domains. Maybe say “for many general-purpose tasks, teams increasingly differentiate on serving.”

[14:45] Camila Reyes: Yep, fair.

[14:47] Ben Carter: Ethan, your “not a single winner” is good, but then we still want a headline. Like, “teams can cut p95 cost by X.” But we can’t say that if not in deck.

[14:58] Ethan Wallace: We can say “material differences” without numbers.

[15:01] Jordan Blake: We’ll keep it qualitative in the analyst briefing, then if they want the table we point them to the public page.

[15:10] Markus Klein: Analysts will ask “who’s the audience.” Make it explicit: engineering leaders + platform teams.

[15:16] Camila Reyes: I can add: “built for engineering and platform teams making region and model choices.”

[15:23] Sana Farid: And one more: in methodology, say “confidence language.” Like, “we report variance and avoid over-claiming.”

[15:31] Jonas Weber: I can add one sentence: “We include rerun policies and interpret results within variance bounds.”

[15:36] Jordan Blake: Now let’s do speed round: each person give their best answer to one of the ‘hard questions.’ I’ll call them out.

[15:44] Jordan Blake: Question: “Why should I trust numbers from a vendor?” Camila.

[15:49] Camila Reyes: We’ve published the full methodology and constraints, use repeated runs to quantify variance, and provide reproduction guidance so others can validate. The intent is to be transparent and defensible, not to make absolute claims.

[16:05] Jordan Blake: Question: “Publish raw data.” Jonas.

[16:08] Jonas Weber: We publish aggregated tables and methodology. We don’t publish raw per-request traces or logs, because that can expose sensitive telemetry and isn’t required to reproduce the benchmark at a reasonable fidelity.

[16:23] Jordan Blake: Question: “What if my workload is different?” Claire.

[16:26] Claire Dubois: Then you should measure with your workload. The report is a baseline—useful for shortlisting and understanding typical tradeoffs. We provide a reproduction template and guidance for adapting concurrency and length distributions.

[16:44] Jordan Blake: Question: “How do you handle region routing differences?” Markus.

[16:47] Markus Klein: We report by region explicitly. If your app uses multi-region routing or fallback, you should evaluate that policy. We can help configure routing and canary settings to meet a target p95.

[17:03] Jordan Blake: Question: “Is this only about hosted?” Ben.

[17:06] Ben Carter: The public benchmark is primarily about hosted inference economics, because that’s where list pricing and broad accessibility exist. Dedicated and Private are about predictable capacity and controls; the report still helps because the runtime and serving principles carry over.

[17:26] Jordan Blake: Great. Now: quick critique—where we might get in trouble.

[17:31] Soojin Lee: Biggest risk is implying ‘objective ranking’ across all use cases. We should keep saying: “baseline workloads,” “representative distributions,” “results will vary,” and “repro guidance.”

[17:44] Soojin Lee: Also, avoid naming specific competitors as “worse.” If asked, we stick to what’s in the table and disclaimers.

[17:54] Jordan Blake: Agree.

[17:56] Ethan Wallace: Another risk is the word “invoice-aligned.” It’s good, but might invite them to ask about enterprise discounts. We should be ready: “hosted list pricing for public data; enterprise varies.”

[18:08] Ben Carter: Yep.

[18:10] Sana Farid: I want one more phrase included: “confidence intervals.” Even if we don’t show full stats on every chart, we can say “we look at run-to-run variance and only publish stable results.”

[18:22] Jonas Weber: We can say “confidence bands” in speech, but it’s not literally a plotted CI on every chart. That’s okay as long as it’s true.

[18:31] Sana Farid: Right, we should say “variance bands” or “variance summary.”

[18:36] Jordan Blake: Good catch. Use “variance summary.”

[18:40] Talia Benson: We have 10 minutes left—can we simulate a more adversarial Q&A? I’ll be the analyst and interrupt.

[18:46] Jordan Blake: Do it.

[18:48] Talia Benson: (analyst) “I’m looking at your metric. Isn’t latency/$ just throughput per dollar inverted? Why invent new terms?”

[18:57] Jonas Weber: Conceptually they’re related, yes. We use latency/$ because it maps to the question engineers ask: “how fast can I respond for a given spend,” especially at p95. We also report throughput and cost so people can interpret it from multiple angles.

[19:15] Talia Benson: (analyst) “Okay, then why not just publish tokens/sec/$?”

[19:19] Claire Dubois: Because tokens/sec/$ can look great while tail latency is unacceptable for interactive workloads. That’s why we anchor on latency and include throughput as supporting.

[19:33] Talia Benson: (analyst) “Do you include prompt caching?”

[19:36] Jonas Weber: We avoid special-case caching that would exploit repetition in a prompt set. We use production runtime defaults and document caching behavior at a high level.

[19:50] Talia Benson: (analyst) “That’s vague.”

[19:52] Soojin Lee: (jumping in) We can be more explicit: we do warm-up, we don’t do per-prompt prefix caching tricks, and we keep config consistent across runs. The goal is representative production serving, not a contrived best-case.

[20:09] Jordan Blake: Nice save.

[20:12] Talia Benson: (analyst) “If a customer runs the reproduction and gets a different result, do you consider your report wrong?”

[20:19] Sana Farid: Different results can happen due to workload differences, configuration, or time-of-day variability. That’s why we define the workload and the window. If they reproduce with the same setup and see a large discrepancy, we want to know; we’ll investigate, rerun, and if needed publish a correction.

[20:41] Jordan Blake: That’s strong—commitment to correction is good.

[20:45] Ben Carter: But we should be careful saying “publish a correction” in a way that sounds scary.

[20:50] Camila Reyes: It’s okay. It signals seriousness.

[20:53] Markus Klein: Analysts will like that.

[20:56] Talia Benson: (analyst) “Last one: what’s new here that others aren’t doing?”

[21:02] Camila Reyes: Two things: first, we’re centering production economics—latency and cost together—across regions with explicit methodology. Second, we’re pairing it with operational guidance: how to reproduce, how to interpret variance, and how to run inference in production with rollouts and fallbacks.

[21:23] Jordan Blake: Great. That’s basically the “why now.”

[21:27] Markus Klein: Can we add one line about “deployment flexibility” since analysts ask? Like hosted/dedicated/private.

[21:33] Camila Reyes: Yup.

[21:35] Jordan Blake: Last five minutes—logistics and ownership.

[21:40] Talia Benson: I’ll send updated run-of-show. We have the final rehearsal Monday 9:30 AM PT for 15 minutes. Everyone please update speaker notes by end of day tomorrow.

[21:51] Ben Carter: I’ll sync with Tyler on UTMs and confirm what link we give analysts. Probably the landing page + PDF.

[21:59] Soojin Lee: I’ll push a short “approved phrasing” block in Slack for the team.

[22:05] Claire Dubois: I’ll write the caching/batching bullet list. Also, the “client in-region” sentence because that always comes up.

[22:12] Sana Farid: I’ll provide a variance phrasing that’s accurate but not too math-y.

[22:17] Markus Klein: I’ll draft the SE Q&A—especially the reproduce steps: region header, config flags, what differences are expected.

[22:25] Ethan Wallace: I’ll add the “how to read charts” script. p50/p95, plus the ratio explanation.

[22:32] Jordan Blake: Perfect. Any last risks?

[22:35] Soojin Lee: Just… don’t get baited into naming specific vendors as worse. Stay on “what we measured” and “how to interpret.”

[22:42] Jordan Blake: Got it. Thanks everyone. Ending recording.

(Recording ended)
